title: Analysis of the interplay between glucose variability, microbiomics and metabolomics in patients with multiple sclerosis during relapse and recovery
summary:
Multiple sclerosis (MS), the most common chronic inflammatory disease of the brain, usually occurs in young adulthood and, according to previous studies, is increasingly associated with a sugar metabolism disorder such as diabetes (diabetes). In addition, there is a presumption that patients who have elevated blood glucose levels during the relapse under cortisone therapy recover worse from the relapse. Since a disturbance in sugar metabolism is closely related to an increase in inflammatory cells in the brain, we would like to investigate this connection in more detail. 
To be able to identify the metabolic pathways responsible for this, we will also perform an examination of the microorganisms (e.g. bacteria) of the oral mucosa, saliva and stool, as well as an examination of the metabolome from the blood. Microorganisms in the mouth and gut appear to play a critical role with respect to immune defense, brain function, and sugar metabolism, and thus represent an interesting interface. The metabolome represents the multitude of metabolites that our body forms and transports in the blood. These reflect the particular lifestyle (diet, exercise, stress, sleep ...) and thus allow us to identify processes that may lead to better or worse recovery.
Lifestyle studies offer great potential to find additional therapeutic options, which are not solely aimed at eliminating inflammation in the brain, but also at regeneration.

interventions.name: Approximately 50 patients with multiple sclerosis in relapse will be included before receiving cortisone. These will be followed up prospectively over the recovery period (3 months).
Additionally we recruit 50 patients with MS without relapse under longterm immunosuppressive therapy

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
MS patients in relapse, EDSS <8
Exclusion criteria:
known diabetes
